lessons.title: Personal pronouns
lessons.summary: The little words for people and things: I, you, he, she… You need them in every sentence, starting with the very first hello.

cards.title: When do you need them?
cards.body: Every time you talk about yourself or someone else: introducing yourself at a course, asking a new colleague's name, talking about a friend. German has **two ways to say 'you'**: a friendly **du** and a polite **Sie**.

examples.english: I'm Anna. And who are you?
Where are you from, Mr Braun?

cards.tip: Hello among students and friends? du. Hello at the office or with strangers? Sie.

cards.title: The whole family
cards.body: Singular: **ich**, **du**, **er/sie/es**. Plural: **wir**, **ihr**, **sie**. And the polite **Sie**, always with a capital S, for one person or many.
cards.tip: ihr is the plural of du: friends you talk to as a group.

cards.title: sie, sie or Sie?
cards.body: Three words that look the same. **sie** + verb with -t = **she**. **sie** + verb with -en = **they**. **Sie** with a capital S + verb with -en = polite **you**. The verb ending and the capital letter tell you which one it is.

examples.english: They are called Tom and Lea.

cards.title: er, sie, es for things too
cards.body: In German, things are not always 'it'. The pronoun follows the article: **der** Tisch → **er**, **die** Lampe → **sie**, **das** Buch → **es**.

examples.german: Wo ist der Kuli? – **Er** ist hier.
examples.english: Where is the pen? – It is here.

examples.german: Die Tasche ist schön. **Sie** ist neu.
examples.english: The bag is nice. It is new.

cards.tip: der → er, die → sie, das → es: the last letter matches!

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Don't mix **du** and **Sie** in the same conversation. Write **ich** with a small i (unlike English 'I'). And remember the capital **S** when you mean polite Sie.

examples.english: Excuse me, do you speak English?

games.explanation: du for friends, family, children and other students; Sie for adults you don't know and at work.
ihr is 'you' for a group of friends.

games.prompt: Das ist Herr Müller. ___ kommt aus Wien.
games.english: This is Mr Müller. He comes from Vienna.
games.explanation: Herr Müller is a man: er.

lessons.title: Present tense
lessons.summary: How verbs change with the person. With the present tense you talk about now, habits and even the future.

cards.title: When do you use it?
cards.body: For almost everything at A1: what you do now (**Ich lerne**), what you do every day (**Ich arbeite in Berlin**) and even plans (**Morgen komme ich**). German has no '-ing' form: **ich lerne** = I learn and I am learning.

cards.title: Stem + ending
cards.body: Take the infinitive, remove **-en**: wohn-en → **wohn**. Then add the ending for the person: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.
cards.tip: wir, sie and Sie always look like the infinitive.

cards.title: Small extra letters
cards.body: If the stem ends in **-t** or **-d**, add an **e** to make it speakable: du arbeit**e**st, er arbeit**e**t. If it ends in **-s, -ß, -z**, du only adds **-t**: du heiß**t**, du tanz**t**.

cards.title: sein and haben
cards.body: The two most important verbs are irregular. Learn them by heart: you need them all the time.

cards.title: Stem-changing verbs
cards.body: Some verbs change their vowel, but only with **du** and **er/sie/es**: **e → i/ie** (sprechen → du sprichst, sehen → er sieht) and **a → ä** (fahren → du fährst, schlafen → er schläft).
cards.tip: ich and wir never change: ich spreche, wir fahren.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: **du** always needs **-st** (not 'du komme'). **er/sie/es** needs **-t**. And don't forget the e: er arbeit**e**t, not 'er arbeitt'.

games.prompt: Match the person and the form of kommen
Does the vowel change with du?
games.explanation: du fährst, du sprichst, du siehst — but du wohnst, du lernst, du kaufst.
sein with ihr is seid (seit is a preposition: 'since').

lessons.title: Where the verb goes
lessons.summary: German is strict about the verb's place. Get this right and your sentences instantly sound German.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body: When you introduce yourself, ask a question or answer one, the verb has a fixed seat. In statements and W-questions it is always **position 2**. In yes/no questions it is **position 1**.

cards.title: Statements: verb second
cards.body: Position 1 can be the subject or something else (a time, a place). The verb stays at **2** and the subject moves **behind** it.
cards.tip: Count blocks, not words: 'In Köln' is one block.

cards.title: W-questions
cards.body: The question word (**wer, was, wo, woher, wie, wann**…) takes position 1, the verb position 2, then the subject.

cards.title: Yes/no questions
cards.body: No question word? Then the **verb comes first**, the subject second. The answer starts with **Ja** or **Nein**, which don't count as a position.

examples.german: **Sprechen** Sie Deutsch? – Ja, ich spreche Deutsch.
examples.english: Do you speak German? – Yes, I speak German.

examples.german: **Bist** du Lehrerin? – Nein, ich bin Ärztin.
examples.english: Are you a teacher? – No, I'm a doctor.

cards.tip: Ja, Nein, und, aber sit at position 0: they don't push the verb.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Don't copy English: 'Heute ich lerne' is wrong — after **Heute** comes the verb: **Heute lerne ich**. And no 'do' in questions: just start with the verb.

games.explanation: Statements and W-questions: verb 2. Yes/no questions: verb 1.
Heute is position 1, so the verb comes next and ich follows.
A yes/no question gets Ja or Nein; W-questions get information.
